fixes.explanation: Rain it is, baker. The verse says, “The ground is cracked because no rain has fallen on the land.” (Jeremiah 14:4) Think of a cookie that stayed in the oven way too long, all cracks and no give. That's the ground, and rain is what it's missing.
The herd doesn't come up in this verse, friend. The reason the text gives is plain: “…because there is no grass.” (Jeremiah 14:5) The drought has reached even the animals.

Yes, friend, it's false. The text says the wild donkeys “…stand on barren heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail for lack of pasture.” (Jeremiah 14:6) Pasture is what they lack, not what they find.

You've got it, baker. The prayer says, “Although our iniquities testify against us, O LORD, act for the sake of Your name.” (Jeremiah 14:7) It owns up to iniquities and still asks Him to act. The request is made for the sake of His name.
A king isn't in this verse, friend. The prayer asks the LORD to “…act for the sake of Your name.” (Jeremiah 14:7) That's the request this card is asking about. It points to His name, not to a throne.

Enemies don't show up in this verse, baker. The request is, “…O LORD, act for the sake of Your name.” (Jeremiah 14:7) The verse speaks of iniquities and rebellions right alongside the ask for Him to act.
Other way around, friend. The prayer says, “Indeed, our rebellions are many; we have sinned against You.” (Jeremiah 14:7) Nothing is dodged there. That's a very honest thing to say out loud.
That's right, baker. The prayer doesn't say they haven't sinned. It says, “Indeed, our rebellions are many; we have sinned against You.” (Jeremiah 14:7) It owns the sin, plain and simple.
That's the line, friend. “Yet You are among us, O LORD, and we are called by Your name.” (Jeremiah 14:9) That word “Yet” turns the whole prayer. The hard questions come first, and then this line.
That's not what the prayer says, baker. It says, “Yet You are among us, O LORD…” (Jeremiah 14:9) Among is the word it uses. Hold onto that one.

Being on the way isn't in this verse, friend. The prayer says, “Yet You are among us, O LORD, and we are called by Your name.” (Jeremiah 14:9) Among us is the line that answers this card. I think that's the line to hold onto.
Yes, baker. The last words of the prayer are, “Do not forsake us!” (Jeremiah 14:9) It comes right after the hard questions. I think that's honest praying.
Careful, friend, because that's exactly how the prayer ends. It says, “Do not forsake us!” (Jeremiah 14:9) Before that come the hard questions. The prayer closes with that ask.

That's what He says, baker. “…although they may offer burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them.” (Jeremiah 14:12) Even if they offer them, the answer is still no. The text leaves it at that.

That's the opposite of what those prophets say, baker. Jeremiah says they tell the people, “…‘You will not see the sword or suffer famine, but I will give you lasting peace in this place.’…” (Jeremiah 14:13) Their message rules out sword and famine and promises lasting peace.

Fasting isn't in what those prophets say, friend. Jeremiah says they tell the people, “…‘You will not see the sword or suffer famine, but I will give you lasting peace in this place.’…” (Jeremiah 14:13) The words quoted are a promise of lasting peace. That's the message Jeremiah reports.
